# What we are doing

Lecture 3 made a claim: a GAM earns its keep when a series has **several cycles running at
once**, because each one gets its own smooth term and you can still read the model.

Retail sales cannot show you that — they have essentially one season. So today we leave M5 and
use electricity demand, which has three large cycles simultaneously, and an annual shape that
will break the first model we try.

The business question: you are forecasting daily demand for a grid operator. Being wrong is
expensive in both directions — under-forecast and you buy power at spot prices, over-forecast
and you have paid to keep generation spinning for nothing.

**Suggested time:** ~40 minutes · **You will need:** `pandas`, `numpy`, `matplotlib`, `prophet`, `pygam`,
and `data/processed/electricity_daily.csv` + `electricity_hourly.csv` (run
`python scripts/prep_electricity.py` once).

---

# Setup

```{python}
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import warnings, logging
warnings.filterwarnings('ignore')
logging.getLogger('cmdstanpy').setLevel(logging.ERROR)   # Prophet is chatty; silence it

from pathlib import Path

def data_path(name):
    """Find the processed data file whether you render from the repo root or from
    this file's own folder."""
    for base in (Path.cwd(), *Path.cwd().parents):
        p = base / "data" / "processed" / name
        if p.exists():
            return p
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find data/processed/{name}. "
        "Run `python scripts/prep_electricity.py` from the repository root first."
    )

daily = pd.read_csv(data_path("electricity_daily.csv"), parse_dates=["date"])
hourly = pd.read_csv(data_path("electricity_hourly.csv"), parse_dates=["datetime"])

# Five and a half years is plenty of yearly cycles and keeps every fit under a second.
daily = daily[daily.date >= "2013-01-01"].reset_index(drop=True)

SPLIT = "2017-08-01"
train, test = daily[daily.date < SPLIT], daily[daily.date >= SPLIT]

rmse = lambda a, b: float(np.sqrt(np.mean((np.asarray(a) - np.asarray(b)) ** 2)))
mae  = lambda a, b: float(np.mean(np.abs(np.asarray(a) - np.asarray(b))))
results = {}

print(f"{len(daily)} days — train {len(train)}, test {len(test)}")
print(f"test window: {test.date.min():%Y-%m-%d} to {test.date.max():%Y-%m-%d}")
```

---

# Step 1 — Three cycles, one series

Before any model, look at the three periodicities separately.

```{python}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.2))

hourly.groupby("hour").mw.mean().plot(ax=axes[0], marker="o", ms=3)
axes[0].set_title("hour of day"); axes[0].set_xlabel("hour")

daily.groupby("dow").mw_mean.mean().plot(ax=axes[1], marker="o", ms=4)
axes[1].set_title("day of week (0=Mon)"); axes[1].set_xlabel("")

daily.groupby("doy").mw_mean.mean().rolling(7, center=True).mean().plot(ax=axes[2])
axes[2].set_title("day of year (7d smoothed)"); axes[2].set_xlabel("")

for a in axes: a.set_ylabel("MW")
plt.tight_layout()
```

```{python}
for label, g in [("hour of day", hourly.groupby("hour").mw.mean()),
                 ("day of week", daily.groupby("dow").mw_mean.mean()),
                 ("day of year", daily.groupby("doy").mw_mean.mean())]:
    swing = 100 * (g.max() - g.min()) / g.mean()
    print(f"{label:<14} swing {swing:5.1f}%   min {g.idxmin():>3}   max {g.idxmax():>3}")
```

**Notice:** all three cycles are large — none is a rounding error you could ignore. This is the
situation Lecture 3 said GAMs are for.

---

# Step 2 — The annual cycle has *two* peaks

Look again at the third panel. It does not look like a wave.

```{python}
doy = daily.groupby("doy").mw_mean.mean()
print(f"January  (days 1-31)    {doy.loc[1:31].mean():,.0f} MW   <- heating")
print(f"April    (days 95-115)  {doy.loc[95:115].mean():,.0f} MW   <- mild, nothing running")
print(f"July     (days 180-200) {doy.loc[180:200].mean():,.0f} MW   <- air conditioning")
```

Two peaks and two troughs per year, because heating and cooling are *both* electricity demand
and they happen at opposite ends of the calendar.

Now the consequence. Fit the annual shape with a single sine wave, then with two.

```{python}
t = np.arange(len(doy))
one = np.c_[np.ones_like(t), np.sin(2*np.pi*t/365), np.cos(2*np.pi*t/365)]
two = np.c_[one,             np.sin(4*np.pi*t/365), np.cos(4*np.pi*t/365)]

for label, X in [("one harmonic", one), ("two harmonics", two)]:
    beta, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(X, doy.values, rcond=None)
    print(f"{label:<15} in-sample RMSE {rmse(doy.values, X @ beta):,.0f} MW")
```

**This is the whole argument for a flexible term.** One harmonic can put its peak in summer or
in winter — not both. Adding the second harmonic (a cycle that repeats *twice* a year) cuts the
error by about a factor of two and a half.

Prophet's `yearly_seasonality` is exactly this idea with more terms: a Fourier series of order
10 by default, so 10 sine/cosine pairs. A `pyGAM` spline gets there differently — by bending
freely — but solves the same problem.

---

# Step 3 — Prophet, and an honest benchmark

Prophet wants two columns named `ds` and `y`. That is most of the API.

```{python}
from prophet import Prophet

# Benchmark first, always: same day last year (364 days keeps the weekday aligned).
lookup = daily.set_index("date").mw_mean
sn = [lookup.get(t - pd.Timedelta(days=364), np.nan) for t in test.date]
results["Seasonal naive (364d)"] = (rmse(test.mw_mean, sn), mae(test.mw_mean, sn))

m = Prophet(yearly_seasonality=True, weekly_seasonality=True, daily_seasonality=False)
m.fit(train.rename(columns={"date": "ds", "mw_mean": "y"})[["ds", "y"]])

fc = m.predict(test.rename(columns={"date": "ds"})[["ds"]])
results["Prophet"] = (rmse(test.mw_mean, fc.yhat), mae(test.mw_mean, fc.yhat))

for k, (r, a) in results.items():
    print(f"{k:<24} RMSE {r:7,.0f}   MAE {a:7,.0f}")
```

We turned `daily_seasonality` off deliberately — the data is one row per day, so there is no
within-day variation left to model. Leave it on and Prophet will happily fit noise.

---

# Step 4 — The components plot

This is the payoff, and the reason Prophet gets used by people who will be questioned about
their forecast.

```{python}
m.plot_components(fc);
```

Three panels, one per additive term, each on the scale of the original series. The trend, the
weekly cycle, the yearly cycle — separately readable.

**Notice** the yearly panel reproduces the double peak from Step 2. Nobody told Prophet about
heating and cooling; the Fourier series had enough terms to find the shape.

# Step 6 — pyGAM, and reading the smooth directly

Prophet is a GAM with the time-series decisions made for you. `pyGAM` makes you state the terms,
which is more work and more control.

```{python}
from pygam import LinearGAM, s, f

# s(0) = cyclic spline on day-of-year (basis="cp" makes Dec 31 join Jan 1)
# f(1) = day-of-week as a categorical factor
X_tr, X_te = train[["doy", "dow"]].values, test[["doy", "dow"]].values

gam = LinearGAM(s(0, n_splines=20, basis="cp") + f(1)).fit(X_tr, train.mw_mean.values)
results["pyGAM (doy + dow)"] = (rmse(test.mw_mean, gam.predict(X_te)),
                                mae(test.mw_mean, gam.predict(X_te)))

print(f"effective degrees of freedom: {gam.statistics_['edof']:.1f}")
print(pd.DataFrame(results, index=["RMSE", "MAE"]).T
        .sort_values("RMSE").round(0).astype(int).to_string())
```

Now the partial dependence — the GAM equivalent of the components plot.

```{python}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.2))
for i, (ax, name) in enumerate(zip(axes, ["day of year", "day of week"])):
    XX = gam.generate_X_grid(term=i)
    pdep, ci = gam.partial_dependence(term=i, X=XX, width=0.95)
    ax.plot(XX[:, i], pdep)
    ax.plot(XX[:, i], ci, c="grey", ls="--", lw=0.8)
    ax.set_title(name); ax.set_ylabel("effect on MW")
plt.tight_layout()
```

**Read the left panel and say what it means in words**, the way you would to a grid operator.
Then read the band: every day of the year appears four or five times in the training data, and a
cyclic spline has no ends, so the band is about the same width all year. Name a predictor where
it would not be, and say where its band would widen.

# Before you leave

You should have found that every method beat the seasonal-naive benchmark **on RMSE**, and that
the single harmonic was the worst of the three models.

Look at the MAE column before you move on. The single-harmonic Prophet has a *worse* MAE than the
benchmark it beat on RMSE. Same two models, same holdout, opposite verdict depending on which
error measure you quote — because RMSE squares errors and so punishes the occasional large miss,
while MAE treats every error proportionally.

> **Discuss:** `pyGAM` was given only day-of-year and day-of-week — no trend term at all. Prophet
> was given a trend, a weekly cycle, *and* a yearly cycle with ten harmonics. Yet on this holdout
> the simpler model won, by roughly 12% on both RMSE and MAE.
>
> Give one reason a more flexible model can lose on a held-out year, and name the thing you
> would check before concluding that pyGAM is genuinely the better choice here.
>
> And the operational question: your forecast is for a grid operator who must buy generation in
> advance. Under-forecasting and over-forecasting cost different amounts. Which of these models
> would you actually ship, and what would you need to know first?
